meaning: The bend applied after a neuron's weighted sum. It makes stacked layers non-linear and, on the way back, multiplies the gradient by its slope.
σ(z) = 1/(1+e^−z): squashes any number into (0, 1). Slope at most 0.25 and near 0 for |z| > 4 (saturation), so deep sigmoid stacks lose their gradient. Still used for probability outputs and gates.
Hyperbolic tangent, a rescaled sigmoid from −1 to 1: zero-centered with slope up to 1, but it still saturates.

Rectified linear unit, max(0, z). Slope exactly 1 for positive inputs (gradients pass unshrunk), one comparison, sparse outputs. Units that are negative for every input get zero gradient forever (dying ReLU).
ReLU with a small slope for negative inputs (0.01 by default; PReLU learns it), so no unit is ever completely cut off from the gradient.
A ReLU unit whose input is negative for every example outputs 0 and gets zero gradient, so it never recovers. Usually caused by a too-high learning rate or a large negative bias.
When an activation is in its flat region (sigmoid or tanh far from 0), its slope is nearly 0 and almost no gradient passes through.
The gradient shrinks as it is multiplied by small slopes layer after layer, so early layers barely learn (0.25¹⁰ ≈ 10⁻⁶ for ten sigmoid layers).

The basic unit of a network: a weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias (z = w·x + b), passed through an activation function. Loosely inspired by brain cells; only the 'add up weighted inputs' idea is borrowed.
A learned number that says how much one input matters to a neuron: 0 means ignore it, negative means evidence against. Training adjusts weights to lower the loss.
A learned number added to a neuron's weighted sum: the score when every input is 0. It slides the decision threshold (the line) without turning it.
A weighted sum of the inputs plus a bias. Used as a number it is linear regression; passed through a sigmoid it is logistic regression, which is exactly one sigmoid neuron.
The set of inputs where a classifier switches its answer. For one neuron it is the straight line (hyperplane) w·x + b = 0; hidden layers let it bend.
Rosenblatt's 1958 learning machine: a step-activation neuron trained by the perceptron rule. It can only learn linearly separable problems.
After each mistake, w ← w + η(y − ŷ)x and b ← b + η(y − ŷ): add the input for a missed yes, subtract it for a false alarm. Guaranteed to stop if a separating line exists; cycles forever otherwise.
A dataset whose classes can be split perfectly by one straight line (hyperplane). AND and OR are; XOR, a circle inside a ring and most real problems are not.
Exclusive-or: 1 when exactly one input is 1. Its classes sit on opposite diagonals, so no single line separates them (best 75% of the four points). Solved by one hidden layer.
A layer between the input and the output whose values (features) are not the final answer. It re-maps the inputs so later layers can separate them; its weights are learned with backprop.

A stack of fully connected layers with activations between them. Despite the name it uses smooth activations and backprop, not the perceptron rule. Also the feed-forward block inside every transformer.

One hidden layer with enough units can approximate any continuous function on a bounded region (Cybenko; Hornik, Stinchcombe and White, 1989). It says nothing about how many units, or whether training finds them.
Width adds units (bends) side by side; depth composes layers so pieces multiply. Some functions need exponentially many units in a shallow net but few in a deep one; deep nets are harder to train.
Total learned numbers. A fully connected layer from n_in to n_out has n_in·n_out weights plus n_out biases; add over layers (2 → 8 → 8 → 1 has 105).
Exponential linear unit: z for z > 0, e^z − 1 otherwise. Negative outputs push the mean toward 0 and units never die; saturates at −1; costs an exponential.
Gaussian error linear unit, z·Φ(z): keep the input with probability Φ(z). Smooth ReLU-like curve with slope 0.5 at 0 and a dip to −0.17. Used in BERT, GPT-2 and ViT.
z·σ(z): the input scaled by its own sigmoid (a self-gate). Smooth, never dead, dips to −0.28. Named SiLU by Hendrycks and Gimpel, proposed by Elfwing et al., rediscovered by search as Swish.
Two projections of the same input multiplied element by element: σ(xW) ⊗ xV. The sigmoid branch is a learned 0–1 dial for the other branch.
A GLU with a Swish gate, used as the feed-forward block of most open LLMs: down(silu(gate(x)) · up(x)). Three matrices, so the hidden size is cut to about 2/3·4d to keep parameters equal.
A raw output score of the last layer, before sigmoid or softmax. Only differences between logits matter for softmax; losses should be given logits, not probabilities.
Turns K logits into probabilities that sum to 1: exponentiate, then divide by the total. A logit gap of 1 means a probability ratio of e ≈ 2.72; adding a constant to all logits changes nothing.
Divide logits by T before softmax: T < 1 sharpens, T > 1 flattens, the ranking never changes. Used for sampling text, knowledge distillation and calibration.
Multi-class: exactly one of K is true → softmax + cross-entropy. Multi-label: any number can be true → an independent sigmoid per label + binary cross-entropy.
Subtract the largest logit before exponentiating (softmax is unchanged by shifts) so e^z never overflows; e^89 is already infinity in float32 and e^12 in float16.
Whether a model's confidence matches how often it is right (its 80% answers are right 80% of the time). Big modern networks tend to be overconfident; temperature scaling is a simple fix.
